title: Alif Lam Mim. Pause before a bold promise.
subtitle: Letters whose meaning Allah knows, opening a prophecy

row.title: a prediction
sub: about the news of the day

then: Ibn Kathir refers back to his discussion of these separate letters at the start of Al-Baqarah. {idea}Their meaning is known to Allah.{/idea} Here they open a surah revealed around the time of the migration to Abyssinia, when believers in Makkah were few and pressed. {reward}What follows is a promise about the future.{/reward}
now: You open the Quran app between meetings, half your mind still on email. Three letters you cannot translate. {idea}Let them do their work: they make you stop.{/idea} Before the bold news that follows, give it your full attention.
old: If I do not understand a word, I can skip it.
new: Not understanding is itself a reason to slow down and listen.
try: Before reading the Quran today, put your phone face down and take one slow breath.

title: The Romans have been beaten. Makkah was gloating.
subtitle: The headline everyone was talking about
then: Ibn Abbas explained: the idolaters of Makkah wanted the Persians to win, as they also worshipped other than Allah. {idea}The Muslims hoped for the Romans{/idea}, who followed a Book. When the Persians crushed the Romans, {trap}Quraysh took it as a sign{/trap} that their side would beat the Muslims too.
now: Your rival at work gets the promotion and the office chat buzzes about it. Or a relative who mocked your choices is doing better than you. {trap}It feels like proof you were wrong.{/trap} {idea}A headline is a moment, not the ending.{/idea}
old: Who is winning right now shows who is right.
new: Today's winner is not the final word. Allah decides how the story ends.
try: Think of one situation where you feel you lost. Say: the matter belongs to Allah, before and after.

title: Beaten nearby, but they will win after defeat.
subtitle: A prediction that seemed impossible
then: The Persians had taken Greater Syria, the land nearest to Arabia. Ibn Kathir says the emperor Heraclius {trap}was forced back to Constantinople and besieged there{/trap}. Then the verse made a plain prediction: {idea}after their defeat, they will win.{/idea} Then Heraclius regained the upper hand.
now: The diagnosis was bad. The business failed. The exam went so wrong you stopped opening the results email. {trap}Everyone, including you, has written you off.{/trap} {idea}After defeat can come victory.{/idea} Allah turned around an empire. Your situation is not too hard for Him.
old: Once it has gone this badly, there is no coming back.
new: Defeat can be the setting for a turnaround only Allah can bring.
try: Make one dua today for the situation you have given up on, as if it can still turn.

title: Within a few years. The command is Allah's.
subtitle: Abu Bakr trusted the timeline

row.title: six years
sub: the middle of three to nine

row.title: Allah's word
sub: a few years, as He said

then: When this was revealed, Abu Bakr {idea}went through Makkah proclaiming it{/idea}. Some of Quraysh made a wager with him, before such betting was forbidden. They set six years. Six passed, and he lost. {reward}In the seventh the Romans won{/reward}, within three to nine years as the verse said, and many people became Muslim.
now: You made dua and gave Allah a deadline in your head: by the end of the year. The year ends. {trap}You feel let down.{/trap} {idea}Allah's promise was never tied to your calendar.{/idea} The command is His, before and after.
old: If it does not happen by my deadline, it is not going to happen.
new: Allah's promises keep His timing, not mine.
try: Remove the deadline from one dua today. Keep asking, and let Allah choose the time.

title: That day the believers rejoiced in Allah's help.
subtitle: Two victories on one day
then: Many scholars, including Ibn Abbas, said the Romans' victory came {reward}on the same day as the battle of Badr{/reward}. The believers rejoiced twice over. One man said he saw the Persians win, then the Romans win, then the Muslims prevail over both, {idea}all within fifteen years.{/idea}
now: The day the result came through. The call that the surgery went well. The job offer after months of rejections. {reward}That joy is meant to be felt.{/reward} {idea}The verse just reminds you whose help it was{/idea}, so the joy becomes thanks.
old: I won because I worked for it.
new: I worked, and Allah helped. The joy belongs to His help.
try: Remember your last real win. Say Alhamdulillah for it, out loud, today.

title: Allah does not break His promise.
subtitle: But most people do not know it
then: Ibn Kathir explains this was a {idea}true promise that cannot change{/idea}. Allah had decreed that the side closer to the truth would prevail. {trap}Most people do not know{/trap} His decree in His creation, yet what He does is wise and just.
now: People let you down. The friend who said they would come. The company that promised a raise. {trap}Over time you stop trusting anyone's word.{/trap} {idea}Allah's word is different.{/idea} What He promised in the Quran, the reward, the ease after hardship, will come.
old: Every promise can be broken, so I hope for nothing.
new: People break promises. Allah never does. I can lean my full weight on His.
try: Find one promise of Allah in the Quran today and hold on to it.

title: Expert at the surface of life, blind to the Hereafter.
subtitle: Knowing the outside of things only
then: Al-Hasan Al-Basri, quoted by Ibn Kathir, said some people {trap}could put a coin on a finger and tell its weight, but did not know how to pray properly.{/trap} {idea}They know the outer side of this life well{/idea} and have no awareness of the next.
now: You know the stock prices, the transfer rumors, the new phone's specs, the best deals on flights. {trap}Ask what happens after death and you go quiet.{/trap} {idea}The verse is not against knowing the world.{/idea} It asks whether you know the one that lasts as well.
old: I am well informed about everything that matters.
new: Knowing this world well is not the same as knowing where I am going.
try: Spend as long learning about the Hereafter today as you spend on one news app.

title: Look inside yourself. Nothing was made for nothing.
subtitle: Creation has a purpose and a deadline
then: Ibn Kathir says thinking about how Allah made things above and below shows {idea}they were not created in jest or in vain{/idea}. They continue until an appointed time, the Day of Resurrection. Still, {trap}many deny they will meet their Lord.{/trap}
now: Lying awake at 2am, you wonder what any of it is for. The job, the commute, the bills. {trap}It can all feel pointless.{/trap} {idea}The verse turns you inward: you were made with intention, and there is a meeting at the end.{/idea}
old: Life is just a series of things that happen.
new: My life was made on purpose, and it is heading to a meeting with my Lord.
try: Sit for two minutes today and ask yourself: what was I made for? Write one honest line.

title: Stronger nations came before. Their power did not save them.
subtitle: Travel and look at the ruins
then: Ibn Kathir explains: nations before Quraysh {trap}were stronger, richer, longer-lived, more developed{/trap}. Messengers came to them with clear signs. They rejected them, and their wealth and sons could not protect them. {idea}Allah did not wrong them. They wronged themselves.{/idea}
now: You walk past the ruins on holiday and take photos. Or you scroll the story of a huge company that collapsed. {trap}You assume it could never happen to you.{/trap} {idea}The verse asks you to look at your own life{/idea}: what am I relying on that they relied on too?
old: I am strong and set up enough to be safe.
new: Strength never protected anyone who ignored Allah. Only turning to Him does.
try: Ask yourself one question today: what warning in my life am I ignoring because I feel secure?

title: Mocking the signs led to the worst end.
subtitle: How small evils grow into denial
then: Ibn Kathir links this to the verse, {trap}when they turned away, Allah turned their hearts away{/trap}. Their end was evil because they denied Allah's signs and made fun of them. {idea}It began with their own choices{/idea}, made again and again.
now: It starts with a joke about prayer in the group chat. Then eye-rolling at a reminder. Then you stop going to the mosque at all. {trap}Each step feels small.{/trap} {idea}The verse shows how mocking a thing slowly makes you unable to see it.{/idea}
old: It is just a joke. It does not mean anything.
new: What I mock, I slowly lose the ability to take seriously.
try: If you hear yourself joking about something sacred today, stop and change the subject.

title: He began it, He will repeat it, you will return.
subtitle: The first creation is proof of the second
then: Ibn Kathir says simply: {idea}just as He was able to create in the first place, He is able to repeat it.{/idea} Then everyone {reward}returns to Him on the Day of Resurrection{/reward}, each repaid according to his deeds.
now: You see the ultrasound of a baby, a heartbeat out of nothing. Or you hold a newborn niece in the hospital. {idea}That is the first creation, happening in front of you.{/idea} The One who does that can bring you back. And you will return to Him.
old: Life after death is hard to imagine.
new: I already exist from nothing. Being brought back is the smaller wonder.
try: Next time you see a baby or a seed sprouting, remind yourself: He will bring me back too.

title: When the Hour comes, the guilty fall silent in despair.
subtitle: Despair when there is no time left
then: Ibn Abbas said {trap}the sinners will be filled with despair{/trap}. Mujahid said they will be exposed, and that they will grieve. It is the moment when nothing can be changed anymore. {idea}The verse speaks of it so that people change before it.{/idea}
now: The despair in this verse comes when the chance is gone. {reward}You still have that chance.{/reward} The unanswered message to your father, the prayers you dropped, the money you owe a friend. {idea}None of it is too late today.{/idea}
old: I have messed up too much to fix things now.
new: Despair belongs to the day that has no tomorrow. Today still does.
try: Fix one small thing today that you have been putting off out of shame.

title: The partners they relied on will not speak for them.
subtitle: What you trusted instead of Allah walks away
then: Ibn Kathir explains that the gods they worshipped instead of Allah {trap}will not intercede for them{/trap}. They will reject and betray them, just when they are needed most. And the worshippers themselves {idea}will disown what they once relied on.{/idea}
now: You count on someone or something: the boss who likes you, the reputation, the clever plan. {trap}It all looks like backup.{/trap} Then a crisis comes and none of it can reach the real problem. {idea}Only Allah stands with you in every situation.{/idea}
old: I have people and plans to fall back on.
new: Everything I lean on besides Allah will step back when I need it most.
try: Name one thing you rely on more than Allah. Ask Him today for what you were asking from it.

title: On that Day, people are separated for good.
subtitle: The parting with no reunion
then: Qatadah said this is {trap}the separation after which there is no reunion{/trap}. Ibn Kathir explains: if one is raised to the highest place and another sent down, {trap}that is the last they ever see of each other.{/trap} {idea}The next verses say what divides them.{/idea}
now: Your family gathers every Eid, your friends meet every Friday. {idea}On that Day, each walks according to their own deeds.{/idea} The verse is a reason to help those you love toward good now, while you are still side by side.
old: We will always be together, my family and I.
new: Staying together then depends on what each of us does now.
try: Invite one person you love to do one good thing with you this week, like praying together.

title: Those who believed and did good will be delighted in a garden.
subtitle: The joy on the other side of the parting
then: After the scene of separation, this verse describes one group. Mujahid and Qatadah said it means {reward}they will enjoy a life of luxury{/reward}, honored and full of joy in a garden. {idea}It is for those who believed and did righteous deeds{/idea}, the two named together.
now: You helped your neighbor carry groceries. You prayed even though you were tired after a long shift. {idea}Belief with action, in small ordinary forms.{/idea} {reward}The verse says this is what leads to delight that does not end.{/reward}
old: Paradise is for saints, not ordinary people like me.
new: Paradise is for those who believe and do good. I can be one of them.
try: Pair your belief with one small good deed today, and offer it to Allah.

title: Denying the meeting leads to the punishment.
subtitle: The other side of the separation
then: Verse 15 described the garden. This verse completes the picture of the separation. Ibn Kathir says each will be {idea}repaid according to his deeds{/idea}. Those who {trap}denied the signs and the meeting with their Lord{/trap} are brought to the punishment.
now: Most of us do not deny the Hereafter out loud. {trap}We just live as if there is no appointment.{/trap} The late-night choices nobody sees, the unkind word you never apologized for. {idea}Living ready for the meeting is the answer to this verse{/idea}, and it starts today.
old: I believe in the Hereafter, so this verse is not about me.
new: Believing in the meeting means living like I will actually attend it.
try: Before sleeping tonight, ask yourself: if I met Allah tomorrow, what would I want to have fixed today?

title: Glorify Allah as evening falls and morning breaks.
subtitle: The day's turning points as times of praise

row.title: just a clock
sub: time to go home, time to wake

then: Ibn Kathir titles this passage the command to pray five times daily. Allah glorifies Himself and tells His servants to glorify Him at times that follow each other. {idea}Night comes with its darkness, then morning with its light{/idea}, and each change shows {reward}His might and power.{/reward}
now: You step out of the office and the streetlights are coming on. Or your alarm rings and grey light is at the curtain. {trap}You reach for your phone.{/trap} {idea}The verse offers a different first move: glorify the One who turned the day.{/idea}
old: Evening and morning are just when my day starts and ends.
new: Every evening and morning are invitations to remember Allah.
try: Tomorrow, before you check your phone, say Subhan Allah three times.

title: All praise is His, from the darkest night to noon.
subtitle: Praise across heavens, earth, and every hour
then: Ibn Kathir says the glorifying of the previous verse is {idea}followed by fitting praise{/idea}. He is praised for all He made in the heavens and the earth. The night time named here is {trap}when darkness is deepest{/trap}, and noon {reward}is when the day is brightest.{/reward} Both are His.
now: The lunch break at noon when you eat at your desk. The late night when you cannot sleep and the house is silent. {idea}Both are moments of His making.{/idea} One sentence of praise turns a blank stretch of time into worship.
old: Praise is for special moments of blessing.
new: Every hour of the day, bright or dark, is a time to praise Him.
try: At lunch today, say Alhamdulillah before you take the first bite.

title: Life from death, death from life. So will you rise.
subtitle: Opposites that show His power
then: Ibn Kathir lists the pairs: {idea}plant from seed and seed from plant, egg from chicken and chicken from egg{/idea}, even a believer from disbelievers and a disbeliever from believers. He revives dead earth with rain. {reward}And so you will be brought out{/reward} of the earth.
now: Your uncle who never prayed now stands in the front row at Jumuah. A child from a quiet home grows into the family's light. {idea}Allah brings life from places that looked dead.{/idea} That includes a heart that feels empty, including yours.
old: Some people, maybe me, are too far gone to change.
new: The One who brings life from death can bring my heart back too.
try: Make dua for one person you have given up on, and one part of yourself you have given up on.

title: From dust, and now you spread across the earth.
subtitle: The sign that is your own existence
then: Ibn Kathir traces the stages: {idea}dust, a drop, a clot, flesh, bones{/idea}, then a soul. A small weak baby grows until he builds cities and crosses seas. He cites a hadith that Adam was made from a handful of all the earth, so {reward}his children vary as the earth varies.{/reward}
now: You sit in the airport scrolling, about to fly across continents for work. {trap}You feel capable, in control.{/trap} {idea}Every skill you have started with dust, then a helpless baby.{/idea} The verse makes your own life the sign.
old: I have earned everything I am able to do.
new: I began as dust. Every ability I have is a gift and a sign.
try: Look at your hands for a moment today and say: You made me from dust. Thank You.

title: He made spouses from yourselves, with love and mercy.
subtitle: Marriage as a sign of Allah
then: Ibn Kathir explains that out of {reward}perfect mercy{/reward} Allah made spouses from people's own kind, so there would be harmony. A man stays with a woman {idea}because he loves her, or out of compassion{/idea}, for their child, or because she needs his care. {idea}Both love and mercy keep a home.{/idea}
now: The argument over dishes again. Then your spouse brings you tea without being asked, after a long shift. {idea}That small kindness is a sign of Allah.{/idea} When love feels tired, {reward}mercy is still there to hold things together.{/reward}
old: When the spark fades, the marriage is failing.
new: Allah put both love and mercy between us. Mercy carries us when love is tired.
try: Do one small act of mercy for your spouse or a family member today, without saying why.

title: Every language and every face is His sign.
subtitle: Human variety as proof of the Creator
then: Ibn Kathir lists many languages of his time and says {idea}only Allah knows how many are spoken{/idea}. Every person has two eyes, a nose, a mouth, and yet {reward}none looks exactly like another.{/reward} Each face has something of its own.
now: On the bus you hear three languages at once. At the hospital the nurse, the doctor and the patient beside you all look different. {trap}It is easy to judge or to not notice.{/trap} {idea}The verse asks you to see each face as a sign.{/idea}
old: People who look or speak differently from me feel foreign.
new: Every different face and voice is a signature of the same Creator.
try: Today, notice one person who looks or speaks very differently from you. Silently say Subhan Allah.

title: Your sleep and your work are both His signs.
subtitle: Rest and earning as gifts
then: Ibn Kathir says among His signs is {reward}the cycle of sleep{/reward}, when people stop moving and rest so their exhaustion goes away. Then He lets them {idea}seek a living and travel by day{/idea}. Signs, he says, for those who listen, meaning those who understand.
now: You scroll in bed until 2am, then drag yourself to work tired and short-tempered. {trap}Sleep feels like something to cut.{/trap} {idea}The verse calls your sleep a sign{/idea}, as much as your paycheck. Rest is part of the design, not a weakness.
old: Sleep is time I lose from getting things done.
new: Sleep is a gift from Allah, and so is the strength I wake with.
try: Put your phone away 20 minutes earlier tonight, and sleep with the intention of rest He gave.

title: Lightning brings fear and hope at once.
subtitle: One flash, two feelings, and rain that revives
then: Ibn Kathir explains: sometimes you {trap}fear the heavy rain and thunderbolts{/trap}, and sometimes a flash gives {reward}hope that much-needed rain is coming{/reward}. Then water revives barren land. {idea}In that is proof of the resurrection.{/idea}
now: A storm warning pings on your phone. The farmer three villages away is praying for it, while you worry about the commute. {idea}One flash holds both fear and hope.{/idea} Your relationship with Allah needs both, like two wings.
old: Either I fear Allah, or I trust His mercy.
new: I can fear Him and hope in Him at the same time. Both keep me steady.
try: In your next dua, ask Allah to protect you from one thing and to grant you one thing.

title: Sky and earth stand by His command, until He calls.
subtitle: One call, and everyone comes out
then: Ibn Kathir notes that when 'Umar swore a strong oath he would say, {idea}No, by the One by whose command the heaven and the earth stand.{/idea} They stand firm by His command. On the Day of Resurrection, {reward}one call will bring the dead out of their graves.{/reward}
now: You stand on a balcony and the city is still there, every building upright. You take it for granted that the ground will hold tomorrow. {idea}It holds because He holds it.{/idea} And the same command will one day call you by name.
old: The world runs on its own.
new: Everything stands by Allah's command, and one day His call will raise me.
try: Next time you stand outside, look at the sky for ten seconds and remember who holds it.

title: Everyone in the heavens and earth belongs to Him.
subtitle: All submit, willingly or unwillingly
then: Ibn Kathir explains that He owns everything in the heavens and earth and all of it is in His service. {idea}All are humble before Him and submit to Him, willingly or unwillingly.{/idea} Even the one who refuses Him {trap}cannot escape His rules{/trap} of birth, aging and death.
now: Your body ages whether you agree or not. Your heart beats without your permission. {trap}In those ways you already submit.{/trap} {idea}The real question is whether you submit willingly{/idea}, with your prayer, your choices, your time.
old: I am in charge of my life.
new: I belong to Allah either way. Let me belong to Him willingly.
try: Pick one area where you resist Allah. Give it to Him willingly today in one small act.

title: Bringing you back is even easier for Him.
subtitle: The highest description belongs to Allah
then: Mujahid said, {idea}repeating it is easier for Him than originating it, and originating it is easy for Him.{/idea} Ibn Kathir cites a hadith qudsi: the son of Adam denies Me by saying I will not remake him as I first made him. {reward}His is the highest description{/reward}: there is nothing like Him.
now: You look at an old photo of your great-grandparents and think, they are gone, dust now. {trap}The idea of them standing again feels too much.{/trap} {idea}Making them the first time was the harder part, if anything is hard for Him.{/idea}
old: Bringing people back from death seems impossible.
new: The One who made me from nothing can easily make me again.
try: Make dua today for one relative who has passed away, knowing you will meet again.

title: Would you make your servant an equal partner?
subtitle: A parable from your own life
then: The idolaters' pilgrimage chant said Allah had {trap}no partner except one He owned{/trap}. Ibn Kathir explains the parable: none of you would let your own servant share your wealth equally. {idea}If you would hate that for yourself, how can you assign partners to Allah from His own creation?{/idea}
now: Imagine your employee demanding half your house and equal say in your family. You would never accept it. {trap}Yet we hand our hopes and fears to people and things Allah made.{/trap} {idea}The verse uses your own sense of fairness to show His oneness.{/idea}
old: Relying on others alongside Allah is harmless.
new: Nothing Allah created can share His place. I would not accept that for myself.
try: When you catch yourself trusting a person more than Allah today, pause and ask Him first.

title: They follow their desires without knowledge.
subtitle: When wants replace evidence

row.title: my desire
sub: I want it, so it is fine

then: After the parable, Ibn Kathir explains, Allah points out that the idolaters worshipped false gods {trap}out of their own folly{/trap}, following desires with no knowledge. {idea}No one can guide those whom Allah lets go astray{/idea}, and no one can save them from His power.
now: You want the thing, so you search until you find a voice online saying it is fine. {trap}Your desire chose the answer before you asked.{/trap} {idea}The verse asks: is this knowledge, or is it what I want dressed up as knowledge?{/idea}
old: If it feels right, it probably is.
new: Feelings are not knowledge. I need guidance, not just agreement.
try: Before your next big decision, ask: am I following knowledge or a want? Then make a quick dua for guidance.

title: Turn your face to the faith you were made for.
subtitle: The fitrah every person is born with
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah {idea}created people to recognize Him{/idea}, linking it to the covenant when all souls said, yes, You are our Lord. He cites the hadith: {reward}every child is born upon the fitrah.{/reward} Most people do not know this.
now: Watch a small child look at the night sky and ask who made the stars. {idea}That question is the fitrah.{/idea} Years of noise, screens and cynicism bury it. {trap}You might feel faith is far from you.{/trap} The verse says it is the deepest part of you.
old: Faith is something I have to force myself into.
new: Faith is what I was made with. Turning to Allah is coming home.
try: Spend five quiet minutes today with no phone, just remembering Allah, and notice what feels natural.

title: Keep turning back to Him, and keep praying.
subtitle: How to hold on to the fitrah
then: Ibn Kathir explains turning to Him as {idea}returning to Him{/idea}, and mindfulness as remembering He is always watching. Prayer is {reward}the greatest act of worship.{/reward} When 'Umar asked Mu'adh about the foundation of this Ummah, he named sincerity, prayer, and obedience. 'Umar said, {idea}you have spoken the truth.{/idea}
now: You drift. A busy week, missed prayers, a habit creeps back. {trap}Then shame says it is pointless to start again.{/trap} {idea}The verse uses the word for turning back, over and over.{/idea} Coming back is the whole method, not a failure of it.
old: I have slipped too many times to keep coming back.
new: Turning back is what I was told to keep doing. Every return counts.
try: Pray your next prayer on time, with the intention of returning to Allah.

title: They split their religion, each group pleased with itself.
subtitle: The trap of smug factions

row.title: the Prophet's way
sub: what he and his Companions were upon

then: Ibn Kathir explains that those who split their religion {trap}believed in parts of it and rejected other parts{/trap}, each group claiming the truth. Asked which group would be saved, the Prophet ﷺ answered: {idea}what I and my Companions are upon.{/idea}
now: The argument in the community chat about whose mosque is right. The eye-roll at someone who prays a little differently. {trap}The quiet pleasure of being in the correct group.{/trap} {idea}The verse turns you to the Prophet's way, and away from pride in your own circle.{/idea}
old: My group has it right. The others are the problem.
new: Pride in my faction is the trap. My task is to follow the Prophet's way humbly.
try: Next time you feel superior to another Muslim's practice, make dua for them and for yourself instead.

title: In trouble they call Him alone. In ease, they forget.
subtitle: The swing between need and neglect
then: Ibn Kathir describes how people sway. {trap}In dire straits they call on Allah alone{/trap}, sincerely. Then times of ease come, and some go back to worshipping others alongside Him. {idea}The verse holds up a mirror to that swing.{/idea}
now: Your child had a fever of 40 and you prayed all night. A month later, healthy and laughing, {trap}your prayer is rushed and your mind elsewhere.{/trap} {idea}The One who answered in the night is the One who keeps her well now.{/idea}
old: I pray hardest when I need something. That is just human.
new: Allah is not only for emergencies. The ease is also from Him.
try: Make one dua today when nothing is wrong, just thanking Allah for a calm moment.

title: Enjoy for now. You will come to know.
subtitle: A warning from the One who says Be
then: Ibn Kathir quotes one of the early scholars: {idea}if a law officer said this to me, I would be afraid.{/idea} So what about when the warning comes from the One who only says to a thing Be, and it is? The ingratitude is {trap}enjoying the gift while denying the Giver.{/trap}
now: A traffic officer says you will hear about this, and your stomach drops for days. {trap}Yet the Quran's warnings slide past us.{/trap} {idea}The verse asks you to feel the weight of who is speaking.{/idea}
old: Warnings in the Quran are general, not really for me.
new: If I fear a human warning, I should take Allah's far more seriously.
try: Read this verse once more slowly, and name one gift you have been enjoying without thanks.

title: Where is your proof? Did We send it down?
subtitle: Worship without evidence
then: Ibn Kathir explains this is {idea}a rhetorical question to denounce them{/idea}. Did Allah send them any proof that speaks for what they worship? {trap}They have no such thing.{/trap} They worshipped others with no evidence at all.
now: A forwarded message tells you to read a special dua 40 times for a miracle. A relative insists on a ritual because grandma did it. {trap}It is easy to follow without asking where it came from.{/trap} {idea}The verse asks: what is the proof?{/idea}
old: If it is part of tradition, it must be right.
new: My worship should rest on what Allah revealed, not on habit.
try: Pick one religious habit you do and find out its source this week.

title: Joy turns to pride, hardship turns to despair.
subtitle: The believer's middle path
then: Ibn Kathir says this describes people {trap}proud when given blessings, despairing when hardship comes{/trap}. Except those who are patient in difficulty and do good in ease. He cites the hadith: {idea}how wonderful is the affair of the believer{/idea}, who gives thanks in good times and is patient in bad, {reward}and both are good for him.{/reward}
now: The bonus comes and you feel on top of the world, telling everyone. Next week the car breaks down and you feel nothing will ever go right. {trap}The swing exhausts you.{/trap} {idea}Thanks in the good, patience in the bad: both keep you steady.{/idea}
old: When things go well, I am great. When they go badly, it is hopeless.
new: Good times call for thanks, hard times for patience. Both can be good for me.
try: Today, thank Allah for one good thing and ask patience for one hard thing.

title: He widens provision for some and narrows it for others.
subtitle: A reason not to swing between pride and despair
then: Right after the swing of joy and despair, this verse. Ibn Kathir says {idea}He is the One controlling it{/idea}, by His wisdom and justice, expanding for some and restricting for some. {reward}In that are signs for people who believe.{/reward}
now: A slow month at the shop. A colleague's side business takes off. {trap}You either blame yourself or feel cheated.{/trap} {idea}Your share is measured by His wisdom{/idea}, which means neither the full months nor the lean ones are the final story.
old: How much I have is all down to me.
new: I work, and Allah measures. That frees me from both pride and despair.
try: On your next payday, say: this is from Allah, whatever the amount.

title: Give your relatives, the poor, and the traveler their due.
subtitle: Giving as a right, not a favor
then: Ibn Kathir explains the relative's due as {idea}respect and keeping the ties of kinship{/idea}. The needy are those with nothing, or not enough. The traveler is the one in need on the road. All this for those seeking {reward}Allah's Face, to look upon Him on the Day of Resurrection.{/reward}
now: The cousin you have not called in two years. The neighbor who is quietly struggling since the layoff. The stranger at the station short on fare. {idea}The verse calls what you give them their right{/idea}, not your favor.
old: Helping family and strangers is extra, if I can spare it.
new: What I give my relatives and those in need is already theirs by right.
try: Call one relative you have lost touch with today, just to ask how they are.

title: Giving to get more back does not grow with Allah.
subtitle: What multiplies and what does not
then: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others explained this as {trap}a gift given in the hope of getting back more{/trap}. There is no reward for it with Allah. But what is given seeking His Face is multiplied. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith: {reward}a date given from lawful earnings grows until it is like Mount Uhud.{/reward}
now: The wedding gift you size up by what they gave you last time. The favor done for a colleague because you will need one back. {trap}It is a quiet trade.{/trap} {idea}The verse invites a different kind of giving{/idea}: small, honest, for Allah alone, and watched over by Him.
old: When I give, I expect something back.
new: What I give hoping for a return stays small. What I give for Allah grows.
try: Give one small thing today to someone who cannot pay you back.

title: He created, provides, ends your life, and revives you.
subtitle: Four acts no partner can do
then: Ibn Kathir describes how a person is brought from the womb {idea}naked and knowing nothing{/idea}, unable to see or hear, with no strength. Then Allah gives him everything: clothing, wealth, earnings. He causes death and gives life again. {trap}None of the partners people worship can do any of it.{/trap}
now: Your first salary, your first flat, your own kitchen. It feels like you built it all. {idea}Trace it back: you arrived with nothing, not even sight.{/idea} The verse asks you to see who has carried you from that cot to this desk.
old: I take care of myself.
new: From my first breath to my last, it is Allah who provides and sustains.
try: Look around your room tonight and name five things you did not have when you were born.

title: Corruption spreads by people's hands, so they might return.
subtitle: When sin shows up in the world around us
then: Scholars gave various meanings: withheld rain and famine, killing on land and piracy at sea. Abu Al-'Aliyah said: {idea}whoever disobeys Allah on earth has corrupted it{/idea}, because the earth's good depends on obedience. Ibn Kathir says Allah lets them taste part of it {reward}so they may return.{/reward}
now: The lie at work that poisons trust in the whole team. The shouting at home that makes the kids anxious. {trap}Small wrongs spread beyond us.{/trap} {idea}The verse says each harm we taste is also a door: perhaps they will return.{/idea}
old: My small wrongs only affect me.
new: What my hands do spreads. And every bitter taste is an invitation to turn back.
try: Think of one wrong habit whose effect spreads to others. Stop it for today.

title: Travel and see how those before ended up.
subtitle: History as a mirror
then: After describing corruption on land and sea, the Prophet ﷺ is told to say: travel and look. Ibn Kathir says, {idea}see what happened to them{/idea} when they rejected the messengers and {trap}were ungrateful for the blessings.{/trap} Most of them were associators.
now: You visit a museum full of empires that once seemed eternal. You read about a family business that collapsed after one generation of greed. {idea}The verse turns sightseeing into reflection.{/idea} What would someone learn from your story?
old: History is about other people.
new: History is a mirror. Their ending warns me about my own choices.
try: Next time you see ruins or read about a fallen power, ask one question about your own gratitude.

title: Set your face to the right way before that Day comes.
subtitle: Hurry to good, while there is time
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah here {idea}commands His servants to hasten to obey Him and to do good deeds{/idea}. When He wills the Day to come, {trap}no one can avert it{/trap}. Then people will be divided into two groups.
now: I will get serious about prayer after exams. After the wedding. After the kids grow up. {trap}The list never ends.{/trap} {idea}The verse says: before.{/idea} Before the Day nobody can push back. Today is already before.
old: I will sort out my faith when life settles down.
new: The time to turn is now, while turning is still possible.
try: Pick one good thing you keep postponing and do the first step of it today.

title: Doing good is preparing a bed for yourself.
subtitle: Every deed lands back on its doer

row.title: disbelief
sub: weighs on the one who chose it

then: The verse right after the division of people. Ibn Kathir explains: {trap}whoever disbelieves will suffer from it{/trap}, and whoever does good {reward}prepares a good place for themselves.{/reward} {idea}Each deed lands back on the one who did it.{/idea}
now: You make your bed in the morning and come home to it tired and grateful. {idea}Every good deed is like that, smoothing a place you will rest in.{/idea} The prayer at dawn, the kind word, the hidden charity: you are setting up your own room.
old: Good deeds are sacrifices I make for others.
new: Every good deed is me preparing my own resting place.
try: Do one quiet good deed today and think: I am preparing my place.

title: The reward comes from His bounty, not our math.
subtitle: One good deed, ten to seven hundred times over
then: Ibn Kathir explains: He rewards believers {reward}from His bounty{/reward}, ten times for one good deed, up to seven hundred, as much as He wills. {trap}He does not love the disbelievers{/trap}, yet He is still just with them and does not wrong them.
now: You gave five dollars at the mosque and felt it was nothing. You helped an elderly man with his bags and forgot it by lunch. {idea}Allah has not forgotten.{/idea} {reward}His reward is not a receipt. It is bounty.{/reward}
old: My good deeds are too small to matter.
new: Allah multiplies from His bounty. No sincere deed is too small.
try: Do one tiny good deed today, a smile, a text of thanks, and trust Allah to grow it.

title: The wind arrives with good news.
subtitle: Winds that carry rain, ships, and livelihoods
then: Ibn Kathir describes the winds as {reward}heralds of mercy{/reward}, followed by rain that revives people and land. They drive ships across the sea, carrying trade and travel between lands. All this {idea}so that you may thank Allah{/idea} for countless favors, seen and hidden.
now: The cool breeze when you open the window on a hot night. The cargo ship that brought your phone, your coffee, your shoes across oceans. {idea}All of it rides on winds and currents He sends.{/idea} The verse ends with one hope: perhaps you will be grateful.
old: The wind is just the wind.
new: Every breeze and every delivery carries something of Allah's mercy.
try: Next time you feel a breeze, pause and say Alhamdulillah.

title: Helping the believers is a duty Allah took on Himself.
subtitle: Consolation for a rejected Messenger
then: Ibn Kathir calls this {idea}consolation for the Prophet ﷺ{/idea}: earlier messengers were also rejected, yet Allah saved those who believed. Helping believers is a duty He took on Himself as a favor. The Prophet ﷺ recited this verse with a hadith: {reward}whoever defends his brother's honor, Allah will defend him from the Fire.{/reward}
now: Someone in the office group chat mocks a Muslim colleague who is not there. You can stay silent, or you can say, that is not fair. {idea}The Prophet ﷺ connected this very verse to defending your brother's honor.{/idea} {reward}Allah pledged help to those who help.{/reward}
old: Standing up for someone will just get me in trouble.
new: When I defend someone's honor, Allah has promised to defend me.
try: Next time someone is spoken badly of in their absence, gently defend them.

title: Clouds spread, break apart, and rain falls through.
subtitle: How joy arrives for the one who waited
then: Ibn Kathir explains how He {idea}makes a lot from a little{/idea}, spreading clouds until they fill the horizon. Some scholars said the clouds break into pieces, others that they pile up, dark and heavy with water. Then drops come out from between them, and {reward}people rejoice because they needed it.{/reward}
now: You watch the radar app as a storm builds over a dry summer. Grey clouds pile up, then the first drops hit the window. {idea}Every stage of that is the verse playing out.{/idea} {reward}Allah chooses where each drop lands.{/reward}
old: Rain falls wherever the weather system goes.
new: Allah shapes every cloud and chooses where His mercy falls.
try: Next time it rains, make a dua. Ask Allah for one thing you need.

title: Just before it came, they had given up.
subtitle: Mercy often arrives at the edge of despair
then: Ibn Kathir describes it: they were waiting for rain at its usual time, {trap}but it was late, and a long time passed.{/trap} They began to despair. {reward}Then it came suddenly{/reward}, at their greatest need, and the barren land swelled with growth. It was a tremendous moment for them.
now: Months of trying for a baby. The job hunt that drags past a year. The prayer for a parent's healing. {trap}You stop expecting anything.{/trap} {idea}The verse describes this exact moment: the despair just before mercy.{/idea}
old: It has taken so long that it is clearly not going to happen.
new: Allah's mercy often comes when I have almost given up. Keep waiting.
try: Make the dua you stopped making. Just once today, ask again.

title: Look at the marks of His mercy on the earth.
subtitle: Spring as proof of resurrection
then: Ibn Kathir says the effects of Allah's mercy are the rain and what grows after it. {idea}Allah draws attention to the revival of bodies{/idea} that died and turned to nothing. {reward}The One who brings land back can raise the dead.{/reward}
now: In spring, the park that was brown and muddy all winter is suddenly full of green shoots. {idea}The verse says: look.{/idea} Really look. That is what the return of the dead will be like, and it is happening in front of you every year.
old: Spring is just a season.
new: Every spring is a preview of the resurrection.
try: Find one green shoot or new leaf today and look at it for ten seconds as a sign.

title: One bad wind and they forget all the rain.
subtitle: How a single loss erases years of thanks
then: Ibn Kathir explains: if a wind came and dried the crops they had tended until they turned yellow and rotted, {trap}they would deny all the blessings they were given before.{/trap} He links it to the people who say, {trap}no, we are deprived!{/trap}
now: Ten good years at the company, then one round of layoffs and you are bitter about everything. A great marriage with one hard month. {trap}A single loss rewrites the whole story.{/trap} {idea}The verse asks you to keep the earlier rain in mind when the yellow wind blows.{/idea}
old: This one bad thing means my life is going wrong.
new: One loss does not cancel all the good Allah already gave me.
try: When something goes wrong today, name three past blessings before you complain.

title: You cannot make the dead hear, or the deaf who turn away.
subtitle: When your words do not reach someone
then: Ibn Kathir explains that just as {trap}the dead in graves cannot hear{/trap}, and the deaf who turn away cannot hear, so some cannot be brought back from misguidance by the Prophet ﷺ. {idea}That matter rests with Allah{/idea}, who can make even the dead hear if He wills.
now: You have talked to your brother about his habits for years. You sent the articles, you said it kindly, you said it angrily. {trap}It feels like talking to a wall, and you blame yourself.{/trap} {idea}Hearts opening is Allah's work. Yours is to keep being kind and to pray.{/idea}
old: If I just find the right words, I can change them.
new: I can speak. Only Allah can make a heart hear.
try: Stop arguing with one person for a week. Make dua for them every day instead.

title: Only those who believe and submit truly hear.
subtitle: The listening heart
then: Ibn Kathir says the ones who hear are {idea}those who are humble, who respond and obey{/idea}. They listen to the truth and follow it. That is the state of the believers. {trap}Being deaf and blind to it{/trap} is the other state.
now: Sitting in the Friday khutbah, half your mind is planning the weekend. Same words, two listeners: one is moved, one forgets by the car park. {idea}The difference is not hearing. It is humility.{/idea}
old: I have heard all these reminders before.
new: Hearing truly depends on a humble heart, not new information.
try: At the next reminder you hear, pick one sentence and act on it today.

title: Weak, then strong, then weak and grey again.
subtitle: The arc of a human life
then: Ibn Kathir traces the stages: {idea}from dust to a drop, to a clot, to flesh and bone{/idea}. Then a baby, weak and thin, grows into a strong young man. Then {trap}middle age, old age, grey hair{/trap}, losing strength inside and out. He creates what He wills.
now: You carry your toddler up the stairs. Thirty years later, your daughter helps you up the same stairs. {idea}Your strength is a loan between two weaknesses.{/idea} The gym, the career, the energy: use them well while they are yours.
old: I will always be as strong as I am now.
new: My strength sits between two weaknesses. I should use it for what lasts.
try: Use some of your strength today to help someone weaker: a child, a parent, an elder.

title: They will swear their whole life lasted an hour.
subtitle: How short life will look from the end
then: Ibn Kathir explains the ignorance of the wrongdoers in both worlds. On that Day {trap}they will swear they stayed no more than an hour{/trap}. They mean there was not enough time for proof against them. {idea}That was always their delusion.{/idea}
now: You look at a photo from ten years ago and think, where did the time go? {trap}It felt like there was always more of it.{/trap} {idea}The verse says that at the end, your whole life will feel shorter than an afternoon.{/idea} Use the hours you have.
old: I have plenty of time to get serious later.
new: My whole life will feel like an hour. Today matters.
try: Give one hour today, or even ten minutes, fully to something you would want to have done.

title: Those with knowledge and faith will answer: you stayed long enough.
subtitle: The record of your time
then: The believers with knowledge reply, {idea}as they established the proof in this world{/idea}. Ibn Kathir says they mean: you stayed {reward}according to the Book of deeds{/reward}, from the day you were created until the day you were raised. {trap}But you did not know.{/trap}
now: Every day you lived is written: the long commute, the Tuesday nobody remembers, the night you helped a friend move. {idea}None of it disappears.{/idea} {reward}Knowledge and faith let you see your days now as they will be seen then.{/reward}
old: Most of my days are forgettable and do not count.
new: Every day I live is recorded. Each one counts.
try: Tonight, write one line about something good you did today, as if for the record.

title: On that Day excuses help no one.
subtitle: No going back to make amends
then: Ibn Kathir explains that on the Day of Resurrection {trap}their excuses will not help{/trap}, and they will not be allowed to return to this world to seek Allah's pleasure. {idea}The chance to make amends belongs to this life.{/idea}
now: Today you can still say sorry to your mother. You can still pay back the money, delete the cruel post, pray the prayer you missed. {reward}Excuses fail there, but repentance works here.{/reward} {idea}The verse is a reason to act while the door is open.{/idea}
old: I will explain myself to Allah when the time comes.
new: Explanations will not help then. Repentance helps now.
try: Make one amends today that you have been delaying: an apology, a repayment, or a sincere tawbah.

title: Every kind of example, and still they called it falsehood.
subtitle: When no proof is ever enough
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah {idea}explained the truth and made it clear with parables{/idea} so people would follow it. But {trap}whatever sign they saw, they called it magic and falsehood{/trap}, as they did when the moon was split. Even every sign would not move them.
now: You keep asking for one more argument, one more video, one more answer before you commit to prayer. {trap}Each time it comes, you find a reason to doubt it.{/trap} {idea}Maybe the question is not the evidence. Maybe it is whether you want to change.{/idea}
old: I just need one more convincing reason.
new: The Quran already gives every kind of example. What I need is willingness.
try: Pick one Quranic parable you know and ask what it asks of you today.

title: This is how hearts that refuse to know get sealed.
subtitle: Rejection repeated becomes a seal
then: After describing those who called every sign magic, the verse says, {trap}thus Allah seals the hearts of those who do not know.{/trap} Ibn Kathir links them to people against whom the word of their Lord is justified, who {idea}would not believe even if every sign came.{/idea}
now: The first time you ignored a reminder, you felt a sting. The tenth time, nothing. {trap}That numbness is what a sealing feels like from inside.{/trap} {idea}The good news: while you still feel the sting, your heart is open.{/idea}
old: Ignoring a reminder once in a while does no harm.
new: Each time I ignore the truth, my heart hardens a little. I want to keep it soft.
try: When a reminder stings today, respond to it instead of brushing it off.

title: Be patient. Allah's promise is true.
subtitle: Do not let the doubters shake you

row.title: the doubters
sub: do not let them shake you

then: The surah opened with a promise about the Romans and ends with this one. Ibn Kathir explains: {idea}bear their stubbornness with patience{/idea}, for Allah will fulfill His promise. Do not let those without certainty {trap}unsettle you from your mission{/trap}. {reward}It is truth in which there is no doubt.{/reward}
now: A colleague laughs when you step out to pray. A friend says religion is outdated. {trap}You start to feel shaky, almost embarrassed.{/trap} {idea}The verse tells you: be patient, the promise is true.{/idea} Their doubt is not a reason to lose your footing.
old: When people around me doubt my faith, I start to doubt it too.
new: Their lack of certainty does not have to become mine. Allah's promise is true.
try: The next time you feel shy about your faith in public, do the act anyway, quietly and calmly.
